events.title: Eighteen survivors
events.summary: The last wild black-footed ferrets, at Meeteetse, Wyoming (129 at their 1984 peak), were hit by distemper and plague and the 18 survivors taken into captivity in 1985-87. Fifteen of them, the genetic equivalent of seven founders, are the ancestors of every ferret alive; releases began in 1991.
events.quote: In 1981, a remnant population was discovered near Meeteetse, Wyoming (Clark et al. 1986, Lockhart et al. 2006). At its peak in 1984, the Meeteetse population numbered 129 animals ... all surviving wild ferrets at Meeteetse were removed during 1985–1987. These ferrets were used to initiate a captive breeding program. Of the 18 remaining ferrets captured from Meeteetse, 15 individuals, representing the genetic equivalent of seven distinct founders, produced a captive population lineage that is the foundation of present recovery efforts
events.cite: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (2019). Species Status Assessment Report for the Black-footed Ferret (Mustela nigripes), version 1.0

events.title: Late-glacial decline
events.summary: Genomes of 612 giant pandas show the three Sichuan populations declining continuously from 30,000 to 10,000 years ago, before they split; they then diverged in their histories over the last 10,000 years.
events.quote: The three Sichuan populations (MSH, LSH, and QX) underwent a similar demographic history characterized by a continuous decline before their separation from 30 kya to 10 kya
events.cite: Lan T, Yang S, Li H, et al. (2024). Large-scale genome sequencing of giant pandas improves the understanding of population structure and future conservation initiatives. PNAS 121:e2406343121

events.title: Human pressure, 3,000 years
events.summary: Whole genomes of 34 pandas: after millions of years of climate-driven swings, human activity drove the recent divergence and serious decline of the panda, and has weighed on all three populations for 3,000 years.
events.quote: Evidence indicated that, whereas global changes in climate were the primary drivers of population fluctuation for millions of years, human activities likely underlie recent population divergence and serious decline. We identified three distinct panda populations that show genetic adaptation to their environments. However, in all three populations, anthropogenic activities have negatively affected pandas for 3,000 years.
events.cite: Zhao S, Zheng P, Dong S, et al. (2013). Whole-genome sequencing of giant pandas provides insights into demographic history and local adaptation. Nat Genet 45:67-71

events.quote: The northern elephant seal was hunted extensively and taken by collectors between the early 1800s and 1892, suffering an extreme population bottleneck as a consequence. Recovery was rapid and now there are over 200,000 individuals.

events.title: Sealing near-extinction
events.summary: Sealers hunted Antarctic fur seals almost to extinction from 1775 (South Georgia) through the 19th century; at least four relict colonies survived, each with an effective size of around 150-200. Breeding numbers stayed tiny into the early 20th century.
events.quote: a species that was hunted to the brink of extinction by 18th and 19th century sealers. ... show that at least four relict populations around Antarctica survived commercial hunting. Coalescent simulations suggest that all of these populations experienced severe bottlenecks down to effective population sizes of around 150-200.

events.title: Pelagic sealing crash
events.summary: Hunting at sea cut the Pribilof fur seal herds until the 1911 treaty ended it; with the harvest stopped, the population grew about 8.6% a year from 1912 to 1924, the fastest rate recorded for the species. The source dates the end of the crash, not its start (pelagic sealing grew in the 1880s).
events.quote: Pelagic sealing led to a decrease in the northern fur seal population; however, a moratorium on northern fur seal harvesting and termination of pelagic sealing resulted in a steady increase in the northern fur seal population from 1912 to 1924. During this period, the rate of population growth was approximately 8.6% (SE = 1.47) per year

events.title: Isle Royale founders
events.summary: Two or three wolves crossed the ice of Lake Superior to Isle Royale in the 1940s and founded a population that peaked near 50; after disease in the early 1980s it crashed to 14 and became severely inbred.
events.quote: The island was colonized by two to three mainland wolves that crossed frozen Lake Superior in the 1940s, establishing a population that, at its peak, included approximately 50 individuals ( 23 ). Following a disease outbreak in the early 1980s, the population crashed to 14 individuals

events.title: Scandinavian refounding
events.summary: Wolves were functionally extinct in Scandinavia by the late 1960s; today's population descends from three immigrants, a pair that bred in 1983 and a male in 1991, and is highly inbred.
events.quote: After functional extinction in the late 1960s, a wolf population was reestablished in Scandinavia by breeding three immigrant founders: a pair in 1983, and a second male in 1991

events.title: Ancestral bottleneck
events.summary: Genetic (site-frequency model of 65 genomes): a very strong bottleneck around 234,000 years ago, after which the surviving lineages coalesce quickly; the authors read it as the species' origin.
events.quote: Demogenetic analyses supported a very strong bottleneck for the species occurring around 234,000 years ago, with most remaining lineages coalescing rapidly, which is consistent with a speciation event.
events.cite: Armstrong EE, Khan A, Taylor RW, et al. (2021). Recent evolutionary history of tigers highlights contrasting roles of genetic drift and selection. Mol Biol Evol 38:2366–2379

events.title: Late Pleistocene bottleneck
events.summary: Genetic (mitochondrial and earlier genetic studies): all living tigers coalesce to a bottleneck around 110,000 years ago. A later genome-wide model dates the species' deep bottleneck older, about 234,000 years ago.
events.quote: The recent coalescence to a late Pleistocene bottleneck (circa 110 kya) [5, 8, 9] poses challenges for detecting tiger subspecific morphological traits, suggesting that elucidating intraspecific evolution in the tiger requires analyses at the genomic scale.
events.cite: Liu YC, Sun X, Driscoll C, et al. (2018). Genome-wide evolutionary analysis of natural history and adaptation in the world's tigers. Curr Biol 28:3840–3849

events.title: 20th-century crash
events.summary: Census estimates: from an estimated 100,000 wild tigers around 1900 to about 3,200 in 2009, a fall of about 97%; numbers have since risen to over 5,000.
events.quote: In 2009, the in-situ population was estimated at around 3,200 individuals, with likely fewer than 2,500 mature individuals. This represents a dramatic decline from an estimated 100,000 at the start of the 20th century.
events.cite: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group, Tiger (Panthera tigris) species page, after IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group 2022, Panthera tigris, IUCN Red List

events.title: Glacial decline
events.summary: Genetic (PSMC, four genomes): a slow fall from 13,000–17,000 to about 6,000–8,000 effective individuals between 75,000 and 30,000 years ago, while glaciers in the Asian mountains were at their largest; snow leopards have stayed few for 900,000 years.
events.quote: Reconstructions suggested that snow leopards had an effective population size of 13,000 to 17,000 individuals from ~300,000 to 75,000 y ago and underwent a slow decline between ~75,000 to 30,000 y ago to an effective population size of ~6,000 to 8,000 individuals. This decline is coincident with the maximum extent of glaciation in mountainous areas of Asia during the Last Glacial Maximum (~40,000 to 100,000 y ago) which was well before the global Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 y ago) (57).
events.cite: Solari KA, Morgan S, Poyarkov AD, et al. (2025). Exceedingly low genetic diversity in snow leopards due to persistently small population size. PNAS 122:e2502584122

events.title: Holocene bottleneck
events.summary: Genetic (microsatellites from scat, range-wide): a bottleneck about 8,000 years ago, as the climate warmed and the treeline rose on the Tibetan Plateau. Genome-wide PSMC is too coarse to see it.
events.quote: Snow leopards exhibited low genetic diversity at microsatellites (AN = 5.8, HO = 0.433, HE = 0.568), virtually no mtDNA variation, and underwent a bottleneck in the Holocene (∼8000 years ago) coinciding with increased temperatures, precipitation, and upward treeline shift in the Tibetan Plateau.
events.cite: Janecka JE, Zhang Y, Li D, et al. (2017). Range-wide snow leopard phylogeography supports three subspecies. J Hered 108:597–607

events.title: Asiatic lion near-extinction
events.summary: Historical record: farming and firearms drove India's lions down after the 1700s to as few as about 20 counted on the Kathiawar Peninsula by the early 1900s; today's Gir lions are nearly identical genetically.
events.quote: This remarkable absence of genomic diversity in Indian lions is consistent with their recorded strong population decline after the 18th century, mostly mediated by the advance of agriculture, the increased use of firearms, and other familiar companions of human population (4). These factors brought the Indian lion population nearly to extinction, with individual counts as low as 20 in the Kathiawar Peninsula by the beginning of the 20th century (35).

events.title: Pleistocene decline
events.summary: Genetic (PSMC): of all the big cats the jaguar was hit hardest by the decline that began 300,000 to 100,000 years ago, levelling off about 30,000 years ago at the lowest effective size of any living big cat.
events.quote: PSMC results (Fig. 1B) revealed population reductions in all five species ca. 100,000 to 300,000 years ago, and a second round of decline (most notably for the lion and leopard) between 10,000 and 20,000 years ago, following the last glacial maximum. In the period between these two rounds of decline, the inferred patterns differ among species, with the leopard showing a rebound ca. 100,000 years ago, whereas the lion and snow leopard remained mostly stable (although at very different effective sizes). The jaguar was the most negatively influenced by the initial decline, stabilizing ca. 30,000 years ago at the lowest effective population size among the extant big cats.
events.cite: Figueiró HV, Li G, Trindade FJ, et al. (2017). Genome-wide signatures of complex introgression and adaptive evolution in the big cats. Sci Adv 3:e1700299

events.title: Last-glacial low
events.summary: Puma numbers in both Americas fell from a peak about 130,000 years ago through the last ice age, reaching their small present-day size by its coldest point, 25,000-20,000 years ago. Read from ten puma genomes.
events.quote: Populations on both continents were largest around 130 kya, during the warmest part of Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 5, and then declined throughout the colder MIS 4–2, with populations reaching their current small sizes by the peak of the last ice age 25–20 kya.
events.cite: Saremi NF, Supple MA, Byrne A, et al. (2019). Puma genomes from North and South America provide insights into the genomic consequences of inbreeding. Nat Commun 10:4769

events.title: North American refounding
events.summary: North American pumas are genetically near-uniform: they look descended from a few founders from South America who recolonised the continent around 10,000 years ago, after the late-Pleistocene extinctions. Contested: whole genomes (Saremi et al. 2019) fit pumas persisting in North America better.
events.quote: The marked uniformity of mtDNA and a reduction in microsatellite allele size expansion indicates that North American pumas derive from a recent (late Pleistocene circa 10,000 years ago) replacement and recolonization by a small number of founders who themselves originated from a centrum of puma genetic diversity in eastern South America 200,000-300,000 years ago.
events.cite: Culver M, Johnson WE, Pecon-Slattery J, O'Brien SJ (2000). Genomic ancestry of the American puma (Puma concolor). J Hered 91:186–197

history.deep_join: PSMC's 2 steps in its blind spot (the last 20 kyr, where it resolves little) are kept, grade D, because Dobrynin et al. 2015, Genome Biol 16:277, Abstract dates a decline there: from the youngest resolved step (~21 kya) to the youngest kept (~11.1 kya, the young edge of the window it dates) the genomic level falls 1.6x. The genome gives the shape, not the number: its curve is scaled ×1.7 to meet the cited 1900 baseline (100,000), then held flat to it.

events.title: Late-Pleistocene crash
events.summary: African cheetahs crashed about 12,000 years ago, when most of the world's large mammals died out at the end of the last ice age. The few survivors left the species with famously little genetic variation.
events.quote: Demographic estimators impute two ancestral population bottlenecks: one >100,000 years ago coincident with cheetah migrations out of the Americas and into Eurasia and Africa, and a second 11,084–12,589 years ago in Africa coincident with late Pleistocene large mammal extinctions.

events.title: Ancient lynx decline
events.summary: Genetic (PSMC): the deepest and most drastic fall in effective size, shared with the Eurasian lynx, between about 700,000 and 100,000 years ago; it may be what split the two species.
events.quote: PSMC inferred a first and most drastic population decline that affected both Iberian and Eurasian lynx 700–100 thousand years ago (kya; Fig. 1b); this contraction may have separated the two species, resulting in the onset of the population structure detected by CoalHMM (312.2 kya; 95% confidence interval 323.1–179.4 kya).
events.cite: Abascal F, Corvelo A, Cruz F, et al. (2016). Extreme genomic erosion after recurrent demographic bottlenecks in the highly endangered Iberian lynx. Genome Biol 17:251

events.title: Glacial bottleneck
events.summary: Genetic (allele-frequency model): an abrupt bottleneck around 47,000 years ago, in the last glaciation, cut the population to about a tenth of its size.
events.quote: Based on the allele frequency spectrum, ∂a∂i infers a model with two successive abrupt bottlenecks, one around 47 kya, coincident with the last important decline observed in PSMC output, and a second one at 315 years ago, both reducing to approximately one-tenth the previous population size.
events.cite: Abascal F, Corvelo A, Cruz F, et al. (2016). Extreme genomic erosion after recurrent demographic bottlenecks in the highly endangered Iberian lynx. Genome Biol 17:251, Fig. 1c

events.title: Early-modern bottleneck
events.summary: Genetic (allele-frequency model): about 315 years before the 2016 study (around 1700) the effective size fell to under 300, in a time of spreading farming, forest loss and persecution.
events.quote: The analysis with ∂a∂i was able to capture a third, more recent decline that reduced the Iberian lynx effective population size to less than 300 individuals around 315 years ago (Fig. 1c).
events.cite: Abascal F, Corvelo A, Cruz F, et al. (2016). Extreme genomic erosion after recurrent demographic bottlenecks in the highly endangered Iberian lynx. Genome Biol 17:251

events.title: Fewer than 100 left
events.summary: Census: a steep decline in the second half of the 20th century left under 100 lynx (under 62 mature) in two isolated Andalusian populations by 2002; conservation has since brought numbers back above 2,000.
events.quote: a steep decline during the second half of the 20th century left less than 100 lynx (less than 62 mature) distributed in the two isolated populations of Doñana and Andújar (Sierra Morena) in Andalusia, southern Spain, leading to its recognition as the most endangered felid in the world [8] and to its classification as “critically endangered” in the 2002, 2006, and 2008 IUCN red lists.
events.cite: Abascal F, Corvelo A, Cruz F, et al. (2016). Extreme genomic erosion after recurrent demographic bottlenecks in the highly endangered Iberian lynx. Genome Biol 17:251

events.title: European extirpation
events.summary: Historical record: extermination policies around 1900 wiped the lynx out of most of central, western and southern Europe; the remnants (Norway, NE Poland, Carpathians, Balkans) passed through extreme bottlenecks, Norway's down to a few survivors from 1926 to 1965.
events.quote: The remnant central European populations recovered from their rather extreme bottlenecks following legal protection enacted during the 20th century, but have remained relatively isolated until today. ... In Norway, the population was restricted to a few survivors in the central region from 1926 to 1965, although it has steadily recovered since then, apparently with little contribution of immigrants from outside Scandinavia (Linnell, Broseth, Odden, & Nilsen, 2010).
